The best sample of the formulations was later used to produce the brake pads. Steel backing plate of pathfinder jeep was selected, surface smoothened, smeared with binder to ensure proper sticking of lining to the backing plate and positioned into the mould. The mixture for the brake pad was compacted on backing plate inside the fabricated mould cavity of pathfinder jeep until the shape was formed and later subjected to heat at 150 oC for about 10 minutes inside an electric furnace where curing process occurred. It was hot pressed immediately after being removed from the furnace using hydraulic press to a certain pressure with about 30 to 45 seconds of pressing which induced curing at that pressure and temperature. It was re-sintered for another 10 minutes, removed from furnace and hot pressed second time. The brake pad was later removed and the edges trimmed to a desirable shape and subsequently allowed cool naturally for about 3 days. The finishing of the brake pad, including grinding and smoothening was carried out to a standard size of 16 mm thickness and all resinous layers were removed using emery cloth made of silicon carbide. The brake pad was then tempered at a temperature 25 oC for about ten minutes to remove the residual stresses induced during finishing process. This process and procedure described above was repeated for all the experimental sets. The produced samples were examined for Brinell hardness test using a universal tester model Gunt WP 300 with maximum test force 20 kN and compressive test using equipment of BS240, a Tensometer M500-25 kN, wear resistance test using a polishing machine model DAP-2 struers with variable speed 0-250 rpm, coefficient of friction test using an incline plane apparatus model 12558, flame resistance, water absorption and oil absorption. SEM were studied using a TESCAN JEOL JEM-7600F scanning electron microscope (SEM), operated at an accelerating voltage of 5-20 kV. The wear rate experiment was accomplished by consistently pressing the samples against a pin on disc rotating machine (silicon carbide paper) of grade 800 fixed on the rotating polishing machine of 180 mm diameter at a constant speed 125 rpm for 2 minutes, under a load of 10 N through a sliding distance of 2000 m. The initial weight of the samples was measured using a single pan electronic weighing machine with an accuracy of 0.01 g. During the test, the pin was pressed against the counterpart rotating cast iron disc of Rockwell hardness 65 HRC and counter surface roughness 0.3μm, by applying the load. A friction detecting arm connected to a strain gauge held and loaded the pin samples vertically into the rotating hardened cast iron disc. After running through a fixed sliding distance, the samples were removed, cleaned with acetone, dried, and weighed to determine the weight loss due to wear. The difference in weight measured before and after the tests give the wear of the samples and the wear rate was calculated using Equation 1.

Appraisal of the developed pks-silica and steel slag brake pad with others Comparison of the physical and mechanical properties of the developed PKS-silica and steel slag brake pad with existing brake pads in literature is shown in Table 7. The wear rate of the newly developed PKS-silica brake pad shows improved wear rate, compressive strength, water absorption rate and hardness compared to existing PKS, other laboratory developed brake pads and commercial brake pad and in addition, the constituents of the developed PKS-silica brake pads have no adverse effect on the environment and pose no health risks as compared to asbestosbased brake pad. The best particle size obtained from the work of Yawas et al. [23] and Chinedu [24] was 125 µm while this research achieved 100 µm, tending towards nano size which enhanced quality performance. Aside that, with the composition of PKS which is half of the lining constituent materials, including silica and steel slag of relative weights will reduce its cost and improve the quality compare to the existing local PKS based pads in the market having up to eight (8) lining materials. As a matter of fact, the eco-friendly nature of PKS has tremendously encouraged its usage in many areas such as asphalt stabilization in road and construction works, and so on.

However, steel slag with less percentage composition of vanadium is encouraged for the development of brake pads in order to prevent the formation of toxic pentavalent oxide form of vanadium (V2O5) in the environment.

Conclusion This research investigated the role of palm kernel shell (PKS) and silica as friction lining materials among steel slag and phenolic resin particles in automotive brake pad production. Hence, this work reached conclusions that the higher the PKS and the lower the silica sand concentrations of the formulated brake pads, the higher the brinell hardness, compressive strength and wear rate while flame resistance, water and oil absorption decreased. PKS, silica sand, steel slag, carbon black and phenolic resin with composition 50%, 10%, 15%, 5% and 20% respectively in formulation B showed the best mechanical property with the lowest particle size 100 μm as compared to others previously obtained. Hardness, compressive strength and wear resistance decreased with increase in particle size, while, flame resistance, oil and water absorption increased with increase in particle size. The coefficient of friction decreased as the particle size increased, the highest coefficient of friction with 100 µm of 0.44 was established. Scanning electron microscope structures of the produced brake pads were analyzed and found to conform to the standard as they show a uniform distribution of resin and the lining materials. The energy dispersive X-ray showed no traces of heavy metal and contain the essential elements such as Al, Fe, Na, O and C among others which are the predominant elements of a good brake pad. 5. Recommendations Based on the results obtained from this research work, it is hereby recommended that the Nigerian government should invest massively in the production of automotive brake pad using composite from palm kernel shell base material, silica sand and slag in order to reduce importation of asbestos brake pads, create employment and diversion of steel slag from landfill.

Modelling the wear processes of the automotive brake pad and disc

The automotive disc braking system is based on the friction between a disc and two pads and this friction determines their wear. The theoretical study proposed in this paper aims to model this wear process. It is based on a simplified geometrical model (approximation of the curvilinear trapezium with a rectangle of the same area) and considering the brake pad as a viscoelastic material, while the disc is elastic. With the help of this model we can determine the relative displacements of the pad and of the disc during the braking process. Also, when the process is stabilized, the pressure distribution can be determined. In the paper, both the relative displacements and the pressure distribution are exemplified for the inner edge, the middle and the outer edge of the brake pad.

Key Words: wear, friction, automotive brake system, brake pad, brake disc 1. INTRODUCTION The braking system is one of the most important safety systems of the vehicle [1]-[3]. Automotive disc brakes are based on the friction between a stator (brake pad) and a rotor (brake disc) in order to transform the kinetic energy transmitted to the wheels in thermal energy. Thus, the tribological study of the brake systems is of utmost importance in their analysis [1], [4-6].

The brake pads are an essential element in the operation of the brake system. They are subjected to very high compressive and shear stresses and pressures of up to 10 MPa. Also, they are subjected to cyclical mechanical and thermal stresses, thus being exposed to fatigue. All these stresses that brake pads are subjected to determine the wear of the pad friction material. Brake pads wear is normal because they are designed to wear out more quickly than discs. Pad wear is influenced by the contact pressure, the relative sliding speed between the disc and the pads and by the temperature of the surfaces in contact [7]. The wear mechanism of the brake pad friction material is a complex phenomenon, being composed of many types of wear: abrasive, adhesive, superficial fatigue and thermal fatigue [6], [8]. Like brake pads, the brake discs are designed to be taken out of use when they have reached the wear limit and will have a thickness below that prescribed by the manufacturers. CONCLUSIONS The current theoretical study, that models the wear process of the brake pad friction material and the brake disc, allows the estimation of the relative deformations of the viscoelastic brake pad in the normal direction with respect to the contact surface and the brake disk. Thus, it has been observed that the relative deformations of the brake pad and disc are higher around the inner diameter than around the outer diameter.

This can be explained by the fact that the pressure is higher on the inner edge than on the outer edge of the pad, its maximum value being in the central area of the inner edge. It has been demonstrated that in a stable regime the wear of the pad and of the disc has a linear dependence of time and its value can be calculated when the friction coefficients of the pad and of the disc are known.

Recent Progress and Evolution in the Development of Non-Asbestos Based Automotive Brake Pad- A Review

Asbestos has been a significant reinforcement material in the production of automobile friction components due to its physical and mechanical properties. However, the replacement of asbestos and other toxic metals employed in producing conventional friction components has been called for due to health and environmental concerns. Research in this area has led to the development of more efficient non-asbestos based organic friction materials for automobiles. In this study, recent progress in the manufacture of non-asbestos based, eco-friendly automotive brake pads is reviewed. A complete classification of conventional and non-conventional friction materials used in the development of brake pads is presented, and the production method and the roles of friction materials

Modern light-duty vehicles have a rear drum and front disc brake system. The brake consists of a caliper with two flat brake pad on either side which presses against a rotating disc when a braking force is applied as shown in Figure 1. The rotor is connected to and rotated with the hub carrying the wheel. The caliper which houses the brake pad provide the means for forcing the pads into contact with rotor. It causes friction which transforms the kinetic energy of the disc to heat energy.

Brake is an important safety component in automobiles. It is applied to stop or retard the motion of vehicles. The life of vehicle occupants and road users depends mainly on the functionality of the brake; therefore brakes must always be reliable and efficient [1-2]. Evolution in the design of brake systems, brake linings and brake pads depend primarily on the physicochemical properties of the materials composing the brake linings and pads. Camel hair, cotton fibers and elm wood were the earliest materials used in automobiles (vehicles produced between 1890 and 1910) before the introduction of cotton-based material composites [3]. Friction materials should be able to absorb and dissipate heat to the atmosphere and renowned automotive brake industry - Raybestos invented the first asbestos-based automobile brake pad [9,10]. The brake pad is a composite of woven asbestos fibers and brass wire. Herbert Frood also introduced the first asbestos-based brake linings in the United Kingdom in 1907 [11]. Unlike cotton or hair, asbestos fibers possess good physicochemical and mechanical properties [12]. Mechanical and tribological tests on asbestos-based friction linings showed that they could maintain their integrity under high braking temperatures and vehicular speeds [3]. These superior properties of asbestos-based linings encouraged their widespread usage until certain diseases were linked to prolonged exposure to asbestos dust.

This paper presents an up-to-date review of the development of non-asbestos based automotive brake pad. A thorough classification of conventional and nonconventional materials used in the development of brake pad is presented and their roles in the mechanical and tribological properties of the pads are discussed. Furthermore, the performance of selected automobile brake pad manufactured from plants, animals and a hybrid of plant and animal materials is investigated in this study.

Classification of brake pad materials The physicomechanical tribological properties of brake pad and other friction components depend on the properties of the constituents and method of production. Three basic classification of friction materials as identified by Bijwe [37] are metallic, carbon-carbon composites and organic polymeric (resin bonded) friction materials. Figure 2 shows the classification and various subdivisions of friction materials.

Several scientists discredited the use of asbestos material due to its cancerous nature [13-24]. It was shown that prolonged exposure to asbestos dust results in asbestosis [25], mesothelioma and other cancerous diseases [26-31]. Consequently, a ban on the use of asbestos was given by the US Environmental Protection Agency in the late 1900s, which resulted in a great revolution in the automobile industry.

Alternatives to asbestos in brake pad production exist, as reviewed in several scientific journals. Abutu et al. [32] presented an overview of automobile brake pads produced from non-hazardous reinforcement materials. They studied the various production methods and properties of automobile brake pads produced from conventional agro-based products. Arman et al. [33] reviewed the composition of brake pads produced from various agricultural wastes- banana peels, palm wastes, aramid fibres, flax fibres etc. The effects of binders on the tribological properties of the formulation were considered. Also, Lawal et al. [34] reviewed various formulation methods, asbestos alternatives materials and properties of the brake pad composites. They also investigated the effect of a locally manufactured plant gum binder on the tribological properties of a cashew nut shell reinforced brake pad as an attempt to obtain a substantially greenbased brake pad. A survey of different manufacturing methods and characterization of asbestos-free brake pads was conducted by Saindane et al. [35]. The various production and characterization methods, binders, reinforcement materials, fillers, and friction modifiers used to develop brake pads were studied based on the available research publications.

Borawski [36] concentrated on conventional and unconventional materials used in brake pad production and the impact on the properties of the developed brake pad. Other review articles on materials proposed for manufacturing brake pads and other friction components include the works of [3, 37-44]. Metallic brake pads are made from sintered brass, copper, iron steel and ceramics alloys. They are used on heavy-duty trains and high-speed aircraft that require extreme thermal stability. Carbon-carbon composites consist of carbon fibers, and carbon reinforced matrices. They are used in racing cars, high-technology vehicles, trains and aircraft where structural integrity is needed than cost. Carboncarbon friction materials are desirable due to their high friction coefficient, low wear rate, high-temperature resistance, and lightweight. However, they are costly to manufacture.

Organic polymeric (resin bonded) friction materials consist of different organic materials bonded together by resin. They are the most commonly used friction materials on modern-day passenger vehicles. Materials used to manufacture organic polymeric friction components are categorized as reinforcement materials, binders, fillers and friction modifiers depending on the role they play in the braking process [45-47]. materials [87-92]. Modern research involves the use of eco-friendly and readily available reinforcements in manufacturing. Based on the type of reinforcement, organic polymeric friction materials are further divided into asbestos and non-asbestos-based, as represented in Figure 2. Asbestos-based friction materials were widely used in the 19th century due to the unique physical and mechanical properties of asbestos fibers. However, the proposed ban on the use of asbestos redirected the focus of researchers and manufacturers to the use of asbestos alternatives.

Non-asbestos-based organic friction materials are grouped into metal-reinforced friction materials also known as semimetallic (resin bonded metallics) and fiber/shell reinforced friction materials. Semi metallics are asbestos-free friction materials that contain between 30 to 65% metal shavings (copper, steel, brass) bonded with resin. They are best suited for heavy-duty vehicles, although they can also be applied to light-duty vehicles. They have strong stopping power and can withstand high-temperature exposure. However, semi-metallic friction materials are noisy during application with high wear rate propensity. Fibers/shell reinforced friction materials are made from materials like glass, carbon, Kevlar or organic fibers bonded together by appropriate resin. They are commonly used on light-duty vehicles. They are less expensive and produce less brake noise during operation. However, they produce a reasonable amount of brake dust and wear quickly, requiring frequent replacement. Binder holds the composite together under various mechanical conditions. It makes up about 20% volume of the entire brake pad composite [37]. The choice of binder depends on the production process. It is a very important ingredient of brake pad composites as it exerts great influence on the overall properties of the brake pad [48-50]. To achieve desired brake pad performance, binder addition during formulation should be precisely determined as excessive binder reduces the coefficient of friction at high temperatures and significantly increases hardness, while too little binder reduces the durability of the pad [51,52]. Resins are the most commonly used binders in brake pad production. The properties, advantages and disadvantages of various resins used in the manufacture of brake pads are listed in Table 1. Fillers are added to fill up the entire volume of the pad. They make up approximately 10% volume of the brake pad composite. Fillers reduce the overall cost of production without negatively affecting the required properties of the brake pad. Conventional and unconventional materials that can be used as fillers for brake pad production are listed in Table 2.

The mechanical and tribological properties of bast fibers reinforced polymer composites have been investigated [94-100], and it was established that the organic fibers positively influence the performance of the composites. Friction modifiers can be abrasive or nonabrasive. They increase or decrease the friction coefficient and influence the mechanical properties of the brake pad. Abrasive powders like alumina or chromium oxide increase friction co-efficient while solid lubricants such as graphite are added to moderate it. Abrasive like copper are often used to enhance heat dissipation. Standard abrasives used in brake pad production are listed in Table 3.

The review paper presents an elaborate classification of friction materials used in brake pad production, and the production methods and the mechanical and tribological properties of developed brake pad are presented. Organic friction materials are further classified in this study into plant-based, animal-based, and plant-animal hybrid. The paper concerns evaluation of the coefficient of friction characterising a friction couple comprising a commercial brake disc cast of flake graphite grey iron and a typical brake pad for passenger motor car. For the applied interaction conditions, the brake pressure of 0.53 MPa and the linear velocity measured on the pad-disc trace axis equalling 15 km/h, evolution of the friction coefficient μ values were observed. It turned out that after a period of 50 minutes, temperature reached the value 270°C and got stabilised. After this time interval, the friction coefficient value also got stabilised on the level of μ = 0.38. In case of a block in its original state, stabilisation of the friction coefficient value occurred after a stage in the course of which a continuous growth of its value was observed up to the level μ = 0.41 and then a decrease to the value μ = 0.38. It can be assumed that occurrence of this stage was an effect of an initial running-in of the friction couple. In consecutive abrasion tests on the same friction couple, the friction coefficient value stabilisation occurred after the stage of a steady increase of its value. It can be stated that the stage corresponded to a secondary running-in of the friction couple. The observed stages lasted for similar periods of time and ended with reaching the stabile level of temperature of the disc-pad contact surface.

Harnessing molluscan shell waste for sustainable tribology by integrating biogenic fillers in eco-friendly brake pad development

www.nature.com/scientificreports Harnessing molluscan shell waste for sustainable tribology by integrating biogenic fillers in ecofriendly brake pad development OPEN N. Jiyas1, S. D. Akshay1, S. J. Ardra1, Anand M. R. Sekhar1, M. Jayakrishnan1, Indu Sasidharan2 & Bindu Kumar K1 Amid growing environmental concerns over conventional brake pad materials, the need for sustainable and efficient alternatives has never been more pressing. This study investigates the innovative use of waste molluscan shells, naturally abundant in calcium carbonate, as eco-friendly substitutes for synthetic fillers in friction composites. Four shell species (Perna perna, Meretrix casta, gastropod, and Rocellaria dubia) were selected for evaluation, integrated into composite formulations alongside permanganate-treated kenaf fiber as reinforcement. Cashew friction dust and graphene oxide served as friction modifiers to optimize tribological performance. The elemental composition and structural characteristics of the shells were examined using Fourier-transform infrared spectroscopy, X-ray fluorescence, and X-ray diffraction, while thermogravimetric analysis assessed thermal stability.

Five composite formulations, including a control sample with commercial calcium carbonate, were fabricated and tested for physical, mechanical, and tribological properties using a pin-on-disc apparatus in accordance with ASTM G99 standards. The top three formulations were further developed into brake pads and subjected to CHASE testing per SAE J661a protocols, including fade and recovery tests to evaluate frictional behavior, wear resistance, and thermal performance. Scanning electron microscopy was employed to analyze worn surface morphologies. The results demonstrate that molluscan shell-based composites offer a compelling green alternative to traditional friction materials, delivering superior performance in terms of friction stability, thermal resilience, and wear resistance. In particular, the P. perna shell powder additive composites emerged as a standout candidate, presenting an ideal synergy of tribological excellence and environmental responsibility. This research highlights the potential of waste-derived bio-fillers in advancing sustainable tribological systems and paves the way for next-generation eco-conscious brake pad technologies. Keywords Molluscan shells, Tribology, Brake pads, Graphene oxide, Chase friction tester The braking system is a critical safety component in both automobiles and industrial machinery, where any failure can lead to severe consequences, including potential loss of life. At the heart of this system lie the brake pads, whose reliable performance is essential for effective braking and overall vehicle safety1,2. Braking is achieved through frictional contact between the brake pad lining and the rotating disc, converting kinetic energy into thermal energy. To ensure optimal performance, the friction material must maintain a stable coefficient of friction while exhibiting minimal wear. The materials are usually made up of reinforcements, fillers, friction modifiers, and binders3. Fillers, both inert and functional, improve composite stability and lower the cost of production without affecting frictional properties4,5. New research has investigated more sustainable substitutes for man-made fillers6like crab shell powder, which enhances tribological behavior as a result of its composition of calcium carbonate and chitin7. In the same manner, periwinkle shells have also been looked at as a potential hydrogen sulphide (H₂S) and ammonia (NH₃), worsening environmental issues11. The majority of this waste is deposited in landfills or oceans, worsening disposal issues. China, the global leader in shellfish production, disposes of 10 million tons of shell waste every year, with little reuse12. Equally so in Nigeria, periwinkle shells are mainly discarded while only a minority of them is recycled into building materials13. In the Galicia region of Spain, the second largest in mussel production, nearly 25,000 tons of waste shell is produced yearly and goes to account for over one million tons disposed globally14. Due to their high calcium carbonate composition, these shells provide a green substitute for traditional synthetic fillers for brake pad composites, conserving waste and resources15. In the Indian context, substantial shell waste is generated, and from this abundant resource, four prominent molluscan species - Perna perna (P. perna), Meretrix casta (M. casta), Gastropoda, and Rocellaria dubia (R. dubia), have been specifically selected for this study. As members of Mollusca, the most diverse and ecologically vital phylum, these species hold immense economic and environmental importance and continue to be at the forefront of aquaculture and sustainability research16. This study explores the value-added utilization of their naturally abundant calcium carbonate, presenting it as an eco-friendly alternative to commercial calcium carbonate in the development of sustainable brake pad composites17.

Reinforcements play a crucial role in enhancing the mechanical strength and endurance of friction materials18. Over the last few years, natural fibres have proved to be cheap and eco-friendly alternatives for man-made fibres like glass, carbon, and aramid19,20. Among various natural fibres, kenaf (Hibiscus cannabinus)21 stands out with high tensile strength, biodegradability, and light weight, being an excellent reinforcing material for friction materials. Kenaf composites have been found to offer superior thermal and acoustic insulation and reduced environmental impact and carbon sequestration22,23. Natural fibers are inherently hydrophilic, leading to weak interfacial adhesion and reduced mechanical strength. To address this, kenaf fibers undergo chemical treatments to enhance durability, surface roughness, and adhesion. Among the different treatment methods, alkaline treatment using sodium hydroxide (NaOH) is commonly used to remove surface impurities and enhance the structure of natural fibers24,25. Potassium permanganate (KMnO₄) treatment further improves fiber bonding, making the fibers more suitable for high-performance composites. In this study, kenaf fibers treated with NaOH followed by KMnO₄ were used as reinforcements to enhance the mechanical strength of brake pad composites.

Friction modifiers regulate wear rates and braking performance by regulating abrasives and lubricants in the composite. A mixture of cashew friction dust (as an abrasive) and graphene oxide (as a solid lubricant) was introduced in this study to enhance tribological properties. Graphene oxide, with its better lubricating and thermal properties, has been widely recognized as a major factor in improving the wear resistance of polymer composites26. Preparation of friction composites was carried out with pure calcium carbonate (CC) as control filler, followed by four green alternatives: Perna perna shell powder (PP), Meretrix casta shell powder, Gastropod shell powder (GD), and Rocellaria dubia shell powder (RB). All composites were analyzed by physical and mechanical tests, followed by tribological tests on a pin-on-disc machine based on ASTM G99 standards. Based on real-time performance requirements for brake pads, the three best-performing composite formulations were selected for brake pad fabrication and further evaluation27. The fabricated brake pads were evaluated using the CHASE test, which replicates real-world braking conditions in accordance with SAE J661a standards, assessing key parameters such as fade, recovery, and wear behavior across varying temperatures28. Additionally, the worn surface microstructures were analyzed through scanning electron microscopy (SEM), while thermogravimetric analysis (TGA) was employed to determine their thermal stability.

This research represents a significant stride in the advancement of biodegradable and renewable materials within brake friction technology, offering high performance without compromising environmental responsibility. By utilizing molluscan shell powder as a natural filler, the study introduces a sustainable and ecofriendly alternative to conventional synthetic materials, encouraging greener manufacturing practices across the automotive and industrial sectors29. It underscores the immense potential of renewable bio-based compounds in friction applications, paving the way for environmentally conscious replacements for traditional fillers. The integration of marine mollusk shell powders into friction composites marks a meaningful move toward cleaner tribology, fostering innovation in sustainable braking systems while preserving reliability and efficiency. Materials and methods Material collection Different shell species were gathered and processed to improve their material characteristics and enable their refinement into fine powder for subsequent analysis and applications. P. perna30,31 commonly known as the Brown Mussel, is a commercially significant bivalve species found along the west coast of India. It is widely harvested for consumption, and its discarded shells, rich in calcium carbonate, hold potential for sustainable applications in composite materials. P. perna shells, as shown in Fig. 1(a), were obtained from the coastal areas of Thiruvananthapuram, Kerala, India (8.5241°N, 76.9366°E), and their powdered form as illustrated in Fig. 1a. M. casta32 as depicted in Fig. 1b, an edible saltwater clam belonging to the Venus clam family (Veneridae), was collected from the coastal areas of Thiruvananthapuram, Kerala, India (8.5241°N, 76.9366°E). M. casta is characterized by a thick, moderately large, trigonal-ovate shell with a white outer surface covered by a brown or dirty grey periostracum. Its inner shell is white with a distinctive dark purple ray on the posterior side.

Due to its high calcium carbonate content, M. casta33 need to edit shells are valuable for various industrial and environmental applications. The grounded powder form from their raw shells is shown in Fig. 1b. Gastropoda shells, as shown in Fig. 1(c), were sourced from Kollam, Kerala, India (8.8932°N, 76.6141°E). Gastropods, a highly diverse class within the phylum Mollusca, exhibit a wide range of shell structures and ecological adaptations34. Their shells, primarily composed of calcium carbonate, offer potential applications in biomaterials and composite development in powder form, as illustrated in Fig. 1(c).

R. dubia35shells as shown in Fig. 1(d), were collected from Kovalam, Thiruvananthapuram, Kerala, India (8.4010°N, 76.9784°E). R. dubia is a thin-shelled, fragile bivalve species with a modioli form shape and a

Fig. 1. Photographic images of marine mollusk shells and their powders. large anterior ventral gape. The shells, rich in carbonate minerals, can be utilized in various material science applications35. The grounded powder form from their raw shells was shown in Fig. 1(d). The collected shells were thoroughly washed with water to remove impurities and dried under direct sunlight. To induce structural modifications and facilitate the breakdown of the shells into a fine powder, controlled heat treatment was performed. PP shells were heated at 350 °C for 45 min, MC shells at 400 °C for 45 min, GD shells at 550 °C for 1 h, and RD shells at 350 °C for 45 minutes17,36,37. This thermal treatment aids in the decomposition of organic residues and enhances the brittleness of the shells, allowing efficient grinding. Following heat treatment, the samples were mechanically ground using a mixer grinder to obtain a uniform fine powder suitable for further analysis and application, as illustrated in Fig. 1. To ensure consistent moisture content across all powdered samples, the ground material was subsequently oven-dried at 105 ± 2 °C for 24 h.

This drying process was carefully selected to eliminate residual moisture without affecting the chemical integrity of the mollusk shells. After drying, the samples were cooled to room temperature in a desiccator to prevent moisture reabsorption from the environment. This approach ensured uniform and controlled moisture levels in all samples, thereby enhancing the reliability and reproducibility of the subsequent experimental procedures.

The reinforcement, kenaf fibre, is sourced from Go Green Products, Chennai, Tamil Nadu, India. To impart hydrophobicity, mechanical strength, and shelf-life extension, to enhance interlocking properties, and to enhance surface roughness, the fibres were treated with NaOH followed by KMnO₄ treatment. In this research, the kenaf fibre was initially subjected to 5% NaOH for 2 h, washed thoroughly in distilled water, and dried using a hot air oven for 24 h. It was subsequently treated with 0.5% KMnO₄ solution for 15 min and then washed properly with distilled water and dried again for 24 h in the hot air oven24,38. The lubricant, graphene oxide, of 5–10 μm particle size was supplied by Ultrasonic Nanotechnology, Bengaluru, Karnataka, India. Five distinct BFCs/

BPs were developed, each incorporating a unique filler at a fixed proportion of 20 wt%, while maintaining the remaining 80% of the formulation unchanged. The compositions and their details are provided in "Fabrication of brake friction composites (BFCs)" Physical, chemical & thermal characterization of marine mollusk shell powders Density measurement of shell powders was established with a digital density meter. Moisture content was analyzed as per ASTM D2495 with the hot air oven method in order to validate and reproduce accurate results39. Molecular structure in marine mollusk shell powders was assessed by Fourier Transform Infrared (FTIR) spectroscopy in a Thermo Scientific Nicolet iS50 spectrometer. The elemental makeup of shell powders was determined by X-ray fluorescence (XRF) spectroscopy with the Bruker S8 Tiger Series II 4 kW to gain information about its mineral composition. The crystalline structure and crystallinity index of the shell powders were determined by X-ray diffraction (XRD) with the Bruker D8 Advance DAVINCI design for phase identification and estimation of crystallite size. TGA was also done using the Perkin Elmer STA 8000 to test the thermal stability and decomposition character of shell powders under the condition of controlled heating. Such analytical methods overall deliver a systematic view of physical, chemical, and thermal behavior of the targeted materials.

Fabrication of brake friction composites (BFCs) A basic friction test was performed using five different composite formulations, as outlined in Table S1 of the supplementary material. The mixing process was carried out using a high-speed blender set to 4000 rpm for a total of 16 min, following a stepwise approach40 In the initial phase, permanganate-treated kenaf fibers were combined with raw natural fillers and blended for 10 min to achieve uniform volume distribution. Afterward, additional fillers and friction-enhancing agents were added and mixed for another three minutes to ensure even dispersion. Finally, phenol-formaldehyde, serving as the binding agent, was added and blended for another three minutes, completing the meticulous 16-minute mixing cycle. The well-blended mixture was then carefully transferred into a cylindrical mold, designed to conform to ASTM G99 standards, for pin sample fabrication. The moulding process was carried out using a hot compression machine, applying a pressure of 15 MPa at 185 °C for 25 min, resulting in cylindrical composite specimens with precise dimensions of 10 mm in diameter and 40 mm in length, as illustrated in Fig. 2.

To enhance structural integrity, minimize porosity, and ensure optimal bonding, a post-curing treatment was performed in a digitalized hot air oven at 180 °C for two hours. The fabricated brake friction composites (BFCs) were designated as Calcium Carbonate filler additive brake friction composite (CCC), P. perna filler additive brake friction composite (PPC), M. casta filler additive brake friction composite (MCC), Gastropoda filler additive brake friction composite (GDC) and R. dubia filler additive brake friction composite (RBC), signifying their unique material compositions as depicted in the Table S1 of the supplementary material.

Physical and mechanical characterization of BFCs The density of the composite was determined using the ASTM D792 standard. Hardness testing was conducted using a Rockwell hardness testing machine in accordance with the ASTM D785 standard, with a loading range of 10 kgf to 100 kgf utilizing a 0.5-inch steel ball indenter and recording the results on the L scale. The porosity of the composite sample was measured based on the Japanese Standard JIS D 4418:1996. The environmental effect of the friction material was evaluated at room temperature following the ASTM D570-77 standard, using water, salt water, and SAE 20W-40 oil as the testing media. The moisture absorption of the specimens was determined using the oven-drying method. Tribological test: friction and wear study The friction and wear characteristics of the developed friction composites were assessed using a pin-on-disc tribometer following the ASTM G99 standard. The tribometer employed a grey cast iron disc with a 160 mm diameter as the counterpart against loaded pin samples. Prior to testing, the disc surface was thoroughly cleaned with acetone to eliminate any contaminants. The test was conducted under varying loads of 40 N, 60 N, and 80 N, with corresponding disc speeds of 300 rpm, 500 rpm, and 700 rpm, over a total sliding distance of 6.3 km.

Each specimen underwent testing for 700 s on each disc speed, totalling 2100 s on a wear track diameter of 120 mm. The tribological studies in this research involved testing brake pads (BPs) using a CHASE friction tester. Figure 3(a) showcases the fabricated brake pads, produced using a standard mold for passenger cars. Test samples, each measuring 25 × 25 × 8 mm, were cut from the fabricated brake pads for evaluation, as depicted in Figure 3b.

The testing procedure followed the SAE J661a/IS2742 schedule, beginning with a 20-minute burnishing run at 308 rpm to ensure proper contact between the brake pad and the rotor. Following burnishing, the baseline-1 test was performed, consisting of 20 brake applications. The fade-1 test then evaluated friction performance across temperatures ranging from 82 °C to 289 °C, with the rotor heated by an external coil. After fade-1, the rotor was cooled, and the Coefficient of Friction (CoF) recovery was assessed. Wear loss was quantified by measuring weight loss using a digital weighing machine and thickness loss using a digital vernier caliper. The process was subsequently repeated for fade-2, with temperatures reaching up to 345 °C, followed by recovery-2 and baseline-2, ensuring a comprehensive friction performance analysis. Results and discussion Physical, chemical & thermal characterization XRD and XRF analysis of marine mollusk shells The XRD analysis of four marine shell varieties, as shown in Fig. 4, revealed distinct crystalline phases, primarily composed of calcium carbonate (CaCO3) in its polymorphic forms of aragonite and calcite41.

The diffraction pattern of PP exhibited strong peaks characteristic of aragonite, while MC primarily consisted of calcite, as indicated by intense peaks at 2θ = 29.4°, 39.5°, and 47.6°. GD displayed an aragonitic structure similar to PP, whereas RB showed a mixed-phase composition of both aragonite and calcite, suggesting a transitional structural adaptation. Variations in diffraction intensities and peak positions indicate differences in biomineralization processes, with aragonite-dominated shells (PP and GD) exhibiting a fibrous structure, while calcite-rich shells33 appear more compact42. The mixed-phase composition of RB suggests an intermediate biomineralization strategy influenced by environmental factors such as salinity and temperature. These findings highlight species-specific adaptations in shell mineralogy, providing insights into the structural and functional evolution of marine mollusk shells. The XRF analysis (Table 1) of the marine shells reveals significant variations in elemental composition, aligning with the structural differences observed in XRD analysis. The high CaO content across all samples confirms their calcium carbonate (CaCO3) composition, with PP and GD exhibiting aragonite-dominated structures, while MC primarily consists of calcite. PP has a high CaO content (77.705%), essential for maintaining structural integrity, and moderate levels of SiO2 (5.215%) and Fe2O3 (0.277%), contributing to its durability and mechanical strength. In contrast, GD, despite having a similar CaO concentration (77.676%), shows significantly higher Fe2O3 (0.997%), which may lead to increased brittleness. The mixed-phase composition of RB is reflected in its intermediate CaO levels and variations in minor elemental concentrations. The presence of Sr and Mg, known stabilizers of aragonite, is higher in PP and GD, reinforcing their aragonitic structure. Meanwhile, MC shows elevated Ba levels, indicative of calcitic biomineralization.

FTIR analysis of marine mollusk shells The FTIR analysis of the four marine shell varieties as evident from Fig. 5 further confirms their calcium carbonate composition through the identification of characteristic absorption bands. The spectra exhibit distinct peaks around 711 cm−1, 860 cm−1, 1080 cm−1, 1404 cm−1, and 1799 cm−1, which correspond to the vibrational modes of carbonate ions43. The strong absorption bands near 1456 cm⁻¹ and 1499 cm⁻¹ are attributed to the asymmetric stretching of carbonate groups, indicative of both aragonite and calcite polymorphs. Notably, the presence of peaks around 2983 cm−1 suggests organic matrix interactions within the shell structure. PP and GD show absorption patterns primarily associated with aragonite, whereas MC exhibits characteristic calcite bands, reinforcing the XRD findings. The mixed-phase composition of RB is reflected in the co-existence of both calcite and aragonite peaks, suggesting a biomineralization strategy that accommodates environmental influences. Fig. 4. Physical and mechanical characterization of BFCs The physical and mechanical properties of the developed friction composites indicate significant variations based on the type of shell powder additives used. The density values suggest that the PPC composite exhibits the highest density (1.50 g/cc), followed by CCC (1.39 g/cc), GDC (1.36 g/cc), MCC (1.32 g/cc), and RBC (1.28 g/cc).

The higher density of PPC and CCC composites suggests a more compact structure with better particle packing and reduced void content, which contributes to increased frictional resistance and improved wear properties45. Lower-density composites, such as RBC and MCC, exhibit higher porosity and reduced compactness, leading to comparatively lower mechanical strength. The physical and mechanical properties of the fabricated brake friction composites were detailed in Table 2.

Porosity plays a crucial role in determining the strength and stability of the composite. Among the composites, PPC exhibited the lowest porosity (14.51%), followed by GDC (17.57%), CCC (19.59%), MCC (25.09%), and RBC (28.13%) as depicted in Table 2. The reduced porosity in PPC and GDC composites suggests a more consolidated structure, reducing the risk of mechanical degradation and improving overall friction performance. Higher porosity in MCC and RBC may lead to increased air entrapment and lower load-bearing capacity, affecting wear resistance. Rockwell hardness values further validate the structural integrity of the composites. The PPC composite demonstrated the highest hardness (86 HRL), followed by GDC (83 HRL), CCC (82 HRL), MCC

(81 HRL), and RBC (78 HRL) as detailed in Table 2. The improved hardness of PPC and GDC composites can be attributed to their dense structure and reduced porosity, ensuring better load distribution and resistance to deformation under frictional forces. The slightly lower hardness values in MCC and RBC indicate relatively lower wear resistance, potentially due to the increased presence of voids and reduced particle bonding strength.

The water absorption and saltwater absorption results indicate that PPC and CCC composites exhibit the lowest water absorption values (14.42% and 15.13%, respectively), while RBC showed the highest absorption (29.36%). Similar trends were observed in saltwater absorption, with PPC (15.48%) and CCC (15.61%) demonstrating superior resistance compared to MCC (25.75%) and RBC (26.90%) as evident from Table 2. The lower absorption capacities of PPC and CCC can be attributed to their compact structure, reduced porosity, and strong interfacial bonding, which minimizes moisture penetration and enhances dimensional stability. The higher absorption values in RBC and MCC are due to their higher porosity, which allows moisture ingress and affects long-term durability. Oil absorption properties follow a similar trend, with PPC exhibiting the lowest absorption (5.83%) and RBC showing the highest (8.56%). The lower oil absorption in PPC and CCC composites enhances their resistance to contamination and degradation, which is crucial for maintaining friction stability and preventing unwanted lubrication effects in brake applications. Moisture content analysis as depicted in Table 2, reveals that PPC (0.28%) and GDC (0.51%) composites have the least moisture retention, followed by MCC (1.38%), RBC (1.26%), and CCC (1.77%). Lower moisture retention in PPC and GDC enhances ingredient interaction and promotes hydrophobicity, improving the thermal and mechanical stability of the composites. The reinforcement effects of Raw Kenaf Fibers (RKF) and Permanganate-treated Kenaf Fibers (PKF) further demonstrate the impact of chemical modification on composite performance. PKF exhibits a significantly higher density (0.87 g/cc) than RKF (0.32 g/cc), indicating an improvement in compactness and structural integrity.

Moisture absorption is also reduced in PKF (4.90 g/cc) compared to RKF (5.85 g/cc), which suggests that the chemical modification enhances hydrophobicity, surface roughness, and interlocking between the ingredients. This amendment enhances the efficiency of load transfer, increases wear resistance, and improves the frictional properties of the composite material. In general, the addition of shell powders has a remarkable influence on the properties of the resultant brake friction composites. PPC and GDC composites have improved density, decreased porosity, increased hardness, and lower absorption capacities, making them suitable for use in high wear resistance and dimensional stability applications. Chemical modification of the reinforcement fibers also improves the mechanical properties further, enhancing fiber-matrix interaction and maximizing frictional performance. The research verifies that sustainable shell powders and chemically treated fibers provide a sustainable and efficient option for highperformance brake friction materials. Tribological analysis using pin on disk tribometer The coefficient of friction (CoF) plays a vital role in assessing brake friction composites, as it is significantly affected by factors such as crystalline structure, thermal characteristics, and chemical composition. Experimental findings indicate that CoF exhibits a declining trend with an increase in RPM across all compositions46as illustrated in Fig. 7(a). At 300 RPM, CCC exhibited the highest CoF (0.43), followed by PPC (0.42) and

GDC (0.40). The reduction in CoF at higher RPMs can be attributed to increased thermal energy, leading to microstructural transformations and reduced interfacial adhesion between the composite and the counter surface. The influence of chemical composition, particularly the calcium carbonate (CaCO3) polymorphs, is evident, as aragonite-dominated compositions (PPC and GDC) exhibited superior friction stability compared to calcite-rich compositions (MCC and RBC). The applied load also plays a role, where higher loads result in slightly lower CoF due to increased real contact area, wear debris formation, and potential tribo-film development.

The crystalline structure, particularly the fibrous nature of aragonite, enhances mechanical interlocking and contributes to higher friction stability in PPC and GDC. The CoF plots for all fabricated BFCs under different loads, 60 N and 80 N, are presented in Figure S1 and Figure S2, respectively, in the supplementary information. Specific Wear Rate (SWR) is a critical indicator of material durability, influenced by both thermal stability and the crystalline phases of the shell powders. The results indicate a general increase in SWR with increasing RPM, as detailed in Fig. 7(b), emphasizing the role of rotational velocity in accelerating material degradation.

At 300 RPM, CCC recorded the lowest SWR (1.96 × 10− 5 mm2/Nm), followed by PPC (1.33 × 10− 5 mm2/Nm) and GDC (1.72 × 10− 5 mm³/Nm). The higher resistance of CCC and PPC to wear loss can be attributed to the presence of calcite and aragonite, respectively, which enhance the thermal stability and structural integrity of the composites. Thermal degradation studies using thermogravimetric analysis (TGA) indicate that aragonite-dominated compositions (PPC and GDC) decompose at higher temperatures compared to calciterich compositions, thus providing better high-temperature wear resistance. The increased wear rates observed in MCC and RBC can be linked to their higher porosity and the presence of mixed-phase aragonite-calcite structures, which may lead to inconsistent wear behavior and reduced thermal resistance. The SWR plots for all Fig. 7. Variation of CoF and SWR with varying RPM of disk at 40 N load. fabricated BFCs under different loads, 60 N and 80 N, are presented in Figure S3 and Figure S4, respectively, in the supplementary information. Friction stability (FS) determines the consistency of braking performance under dynamic conditions and is influenced by the structural and chemical composition of the shell powders. CCC, PPC, and GDC exhibited the highest stability, with minimal fluctuations in FS values across varying loads and RPMs which are evident from Fig. 8. At 300 RPM, CCC retained approximately 92% stability, PPC maintained 95%, and GDC followed with 93.2%. The reinforcement properties of aragonite in PPC and GDC contribute to their high stability due to their fibrous microstructure, which aids in maintaining uniform contact interfaces. The chemical composition of the composites, particularly the presence of organic matrices in PPC, enhances load-bearing capacity and minimizes sudden fluctuations in friction response. In contrast, MCC and RBC displayed instability at higher RPMs, which may be attributed to their mixed-phase composition and lower thermal stability. The friction stability plots for all fabricated BFCs under different loads, 60 N and 80 N, are presented in Figure S5 and Figure S6, respectively, in the supplementary information.

The tribological performance of the composites is significantly impacted by the inherent physical, chemical, and thermal properties of the shell powders. CCC, which utilizes calcium carbonate (CaCO3) in calcite form, exhibited excellent wear resistance and friction stability, largely due to the formation of a protective tribo-layer under high-stress conditions47. PPC, composed of P. perna shell powder with a high aragonite content, displayed superior load-bearing capabilities and enhanced wear resistance due to its fibrous microstructure. GDC, infused with Gastropoda shell powder, maintained stable frictional properties and moderate wear resistance, highlighting its potential as a sustainable filler. The mixed-phase nature of MCC and RBC resulted in higher wear rates and inconsistent friction stability, making them less suitable for high-performance braking applications. The density and porosity of friction composites play a vital role in wear resistance and structural durability. PPC exhibited the highest density (1.50 g/cc) and lowest porosity (14.51%), contributing to superior wear resistance and friction stability. CCC followed with a density of 1.39 g/cc and a porosity of 19.59%, further reinforcing its structural integrity under dynamic loading conditions42. GDC, with a density of 1.36 g/cc and a porosity of 17.57%, also displayed promising tribological properties. The increased porosities observed in MCC (25.09%) and RBC (28.13%) correlated with higher wear rates, as a greater number of voids lead to increased fragmentation and reduced mechanical strength. Among the five tested friction composites, CCC, PPC, and GDC emerged as the best-performing compositions due to their superior CoF stability, lower SWR, and enhanced wear resistance. Their tribological superiority can be attributed to their crystalline structure, thermal stability, and chemical composition, which contribute to effective load-bearing capacity, improved wear resistance, and stable frictional properties. These compositions were optimized for brake pad fabrication and subjected to real-time testing using the CHASE friction test as per SAE J661 standards.

Figure 12 illustrates the wear loss of the developed brake pad, highlighting the superior thermal stability of mineral shell powder, particularly P. perna, in minimizing wear at elevated temperatures. This remarkable stability effectively mitigates wear loss, aligning with the observations of previous studies49. During braking, the intense heat generated initiates tribo-oxidation, leading to the formation of abrasive particles that accelerate wear, a phenomenon consistent with the findings from previous studies55.

The wear resistance of a brake composite is naturally controlled by its hardness, thermal stability, and structural integrity56. Higher hardness increases the resistance to indentation, hence lowering surface degradation under braking conditions57. PPC brake pads had the lowest weight and thickness loss in the tested composites, further confirming their maximum wear resistance and durability. Also, PPC and CCC had little thickness and weight loss, as illustrated in Fig. 12, adding to their potential use in long-term braking.

Kenaf fibers, used as reinforcement in the brake pads, helped in load distribution and strength, improving resistance to localized stress concentration and wear58,59. Furthermore, graphene oxide, employed as a lubricant additive, dramatically improved lubricity, encouraging more favorable interfacing among ingredients60. This helped in superior heat management, mitigating wear and friction-caused degradation. With respect to standard natural reinforcement-type brake pads, the incorporation of graphene oxide into PPC yielded decreased wear rates and improved thermal stability29.

Of the friction composites tested, PPC performed the best, showing excellent stability in the CoF, low wear loss, and high thermal endurance. Filler material selection is a critical factor in what makes brake pads frictional and wear-resistant, and PPC has shown impressive efficiency in this aspect. Its excellent tribological behavior makes it a preferred component for low-to-medium load applications, guaranteeing durability and reliability. With a brake pad Edge Code (SAE J866) of “EE”, PPC aligns well to industry standards, keeping normal and hot CoF values in the range of 0.25–0.35. This makes it especially suitable for passenger vehicles and low-temperature brake use, where stable performance is paramount. Additionally, PPC-derived brake pads present some benefits in the form of noise-free functioning, lower rotor wear, and higher sustainability using biodegradable shell powders52. While maintaining the required braking performance, PPC also demonstrates stable friction behavior, thus supporting its applications in today’s automotive needs. Morphological study Micrographs of the worn surfaces of the test specimens, both before and after wear testing, were captured using a Scanning Electron Microscope (JEOL JSM-IT510). The wear mechanisms in polymer matrix composites encompass multiple modes, including fiber pullout, fiber-matrix debonding, matrix cracking, the formation of matrix debris, and the development of contact plateaus. The SEM images, presented in Fig. 13a–f, offer valuable insights into the microstructural evolution of the friction composites under dynamic frictional loading. Figure 13(a) illustrates the CCC composite before wear, where smaller voids (A) and reinforcement fibers (B) are evident. Figures 13(c) and (e) showcase the GDC and PPC composites, respectively, revealing finely distributed ingredient particles (C) and surface cracks (D) prior to wear exposure. These distinct morphological features are closely linked to the polymorphic composition of the filler materials. Notably, PPC and GDC are predominantly composed of aragonite, a calcium carbonate polymorph known for its fibrous microstructure, which enhances mechanical reinforcement and interfacial bonding strength. This structural advantage translates to improved wear resistance, as the fibrous nature of aragonite provides better load distribution and impact absorption during braking. In contrast, the SEM analysis of GDC composites reveals loosely packed particles near the hard plateaus (marked as ‘E’ in Fig. 13d). The rotary motion facilitates their progressive accumulation and fusion under frictional forces, leading to a denser and more cohesive surface structure (Filip, Weiss et al. 2002). However, Fig. 13(b) highlights irregular wear patterns in CCC composites, primarily due to the synthetic CaCO₃ and sillimanite fillers. These fillers exhibit heterogeneous morphology, which promotes localized abrasions and increased surface roughness. Direct interaction between rotor asperities and these uneven plateaus leads to further material loss, resulting in distinct wear tracks along the sliding direction (marked as ‘G’ in Fig. 13(b)). Moreover, larger detached debris particles (marked as ‘F’ in Fig. 13(b)) are observed, particularly in CCC samples. These fragments originate from weakly bonded filler-matrix regions, reinforcing the critical role of strong interfacial adhesion in wear resistance. The superior wear performance of PPC and GDC composites can thus be attributed to their aragonitic composition, which enhances structural integrity, reduces material detachment, and ultimately improves tribological efficiency in braking applications.

The post-wear analysis highlights the formation of hard (primary) plateaus, marked as ‘H’ in Fig. 13(f), arising from the exposure of stable filler additives, particularly P. perna shell powders, against the rotor surface. These mechanically robust plateaus endure intense frictional forces, effectively reducing material degradation during braking operations61. Additionally, soft (secondary) plateaus, denoted as ‘I’ in Fig. 13(f), emerge due to the accumulation of wear debris within interfacial spaces. As the rotor moves, frictional heat and pressure cause these loose particles to fuse, thereby reinforcing the wear surface and enhancing frictional stability. These plateaus are instrumental in defining the effective contact area between the rotor and the brake pad, mitigating direct interactions between rotor asperities and softer matrix components such as the phenolic binder and P. perna shell powders62. Consequently, this phenomenon contributes to reduced wear and prolonged durability. Conclusions The present study underscores the remarkable potential of mollusk shell-derived fillers in revolutionizing the landscape of brake friction materials by offering a sustainable, high-performance alternative to conventional synthetic CaCO₃-based composites. The inherent chemical composition of these biogenic materials, enriched with calcium carbonate and organic biopolymers, plays a pivotal role in enhancing structural integrity, crystalline stability, and tribological performance. Among the tested formulations, PPC emerged as the most promising candidate, demonstrating superior density, reduced porosity, and enhanced hardness, ensuring exceptional load-bearing capacity and wear resistance. PPC exhibited outstanding tribological stability, surpassing CCC and GDC with a 3% higher coefficient of friction in the range of 0.30–0.35. Notably, it significantly reduced brake fade, with Fade 1 and Fade 2 decreasing by 18.2% and 23.6%, respectively. The predicted normal (0.34) and hot CoF (0.35) values fall well within the industry-recommended range of 0.30 to 0.55, ensuring compliance with SAE J866 Edge Code and OEM specifications. This alignment guarantees exceptional braking reliability, reduced performance degradation, and enhanced driver comfort, positioning PPC as a highly promising candidate for next-generation friction materials. Additionally, PPC’s outstanding recovery rate of 107%, along with its higher decomposition temperatures and reduced material degradation, highlights its superior thermal resilience under dynamic braking conditions. The wear studies further reinforced PPC’s exceptional durability, showing a significant 12.5% improvement over CCC and 9.3% over GDC in wear resistance. The XRD and SEM analyses provided compelling evidence of PPC’s aragonite-dominant crystalline phase, which contributes to its exceptional mechanical reinforcement and minimal material detachment under high-stress conditions. By successfully harnessing waste mollusk shells into friction composites, this research not only advances greener tribology but also paves the way for sustainable innovations in automotive braking systems. The findings affirm that PPC is not merely a viable alternative but a superior choice, offering an optimal balance of frictional

RECENT PROGRESS AND EVOLUTION IN THE DEVELOPMENT OF NON-ASBESTOS BASED AUTOMOTIVE BRAKE PADS- A REVIEW

Asbestos has been a significant reinforcement material in producing automobile friction components due to its physical and mechanical properties. However, the replacement of asbestos and other toxic metals employed in producing conventional friction components has been called for due to health and environmental concerns. Research in this area has led to the development of more efficient non-asbestos-based organic friction materials for automobiles. In this study, recent progress in the manufacture of non-asbestos-based, eco-friendly automotive brake pads is reviewed. Modern light-duty vehicles are manufactured with rear drum and front disc brake systems. The brake consists of a calliper with two flat pads on either side, pressing against a rotating disc when a braking force is applied (see Figure 1). The rotor is connected to and rotated with the hub carrying the wheel. The calliper, which houses the brake pads, provides the means for forcing the pads into contact with the rotor. It causes friction, transforming the disc’s kinetic energy to heat energy.

The brake is an important safety component in automobiles. It is applied to stop or retard the motion of vehicles. The life of vehicle occupants and road users depends mainly on the functionality of the brake; therefore, brakes must always be reliable and efficient [1-2]. Evolution in the brake system design, brake linings and brake pads depends largely on the physicochemical properties of the materials composing the brake linings and pads. Camel hair, cotton fibres and elm wood were the earliest materials used in automobiles (vehicles produced between 1890-1910) before the introduction of cotton-based material composites [3]. Friction materials should be able to absorb and dissipate heat to the atmosphere and invented the US’s first asbestos-based automobile brake pads [9,10]. The brake pad is a composite of woven asbestos fibres and brass wire. Herbert Frood also introduced the first asbestos-based brake linings in the United Kingdom in 1907 [11]. Unlike cotton or hair, asbestos fibres possess good physicochemical and mechanical properties [12]. Mechanical and tribological tests on asbestos-based friction linings showed they could maintain their integrity under high braking temperatures and vehicular speeds [3]. These superior properties of asbestos-based linings encouraged their widespread usage until certain diseases were linked to prolonged exposure to asbestos dust. development. A thorough classification of conventional and non-conventional materials used in the development of brake pads is presented, and their roles in the mechanical and tribological properties of the pads are discussed. Furthermore, the performance of selected automobile brake pads manufactured from plants, animals and a hybrid of plant and animal materials is investigated in this study.

Metallic brake pads are made from sintered brass, copper, iron steel and ceramics alloys. They are used on heavy-duty trains and high-speed aircraft that require extreme thermal stability. Carbon-carbon composites consist of carbon fibres and carbon-reinforced matrices. They are used in racing cars, high-technology vehicles, trains and aircraft where structural integrity is needed than cost. Carboncarbon friction materials are desirable due to their high friction coefficient, low wear rate, resistance to high temperatures and lightweight. However, they are very expensive to manufacture.

Organic polymeric (resin-bonded) friction materials consist of different organic materials bonded together by resin. They are the most commonly used friction materials on modern-day passenger vehicles. Materials used to manufacture organic polymeric This paper presents an up-to-date review of non-asbestos-based automotive brake friction components are categorized as reinforcement materials, binders, fillers and friction modifiers, depending on their role in the braking process [45-47]. Based on the type of reinforcement, organic polymeric friction materials are divided into asbestos and non-asbestos-based (Fig. 2). Asbestos-based friction materials were widely used in the 19th century due to the unique physical and mechanical properties of asbestos fibres. However, the proposed ban on the use of asbestos redirected the focus of researchers and manufacturers to the use of asbestos alternatives. Nonasbestos-based organic friction materials are grouped into metal-reinforced, semi-metallic (resin-bonded metallics) and fibre/shell-reinforced friction materials.

Semi-metallics are asbestos-free friction materials containing 30 to 65% metal shavings (copper, steel, brass) bonded with resin. They are best suited for heavy-duty vehicles although they can also be applied to light-duty vehicles. They have strong stopping power and can withstand high-temperature exposure. However, semi-metallic friction materials are noisy during application, with a high wear rate propensity.

Fibres/shell-reinforced friction materials are made from glass, carbon, Kevlar or organic fibres bonded together by appropriate resin. They are commonly used on lightduty vehicles. They are less expensive and produce less brake noise during operation. However, they produce a reasonable amount of brake dust and wear quickly, requiring frequent replacement. Binder holds the composite together under various mechanical conditions. It makes up about 20% volume of the entire brake pad composite [37]. The choice of binder depends on the production process. It is a very important ingredient of brake pad composites as it greatly influences the overall properties of the brake [48-50].

To achieve desired brake pad performance, binder addition during formulation should be precisely determined as excessive binder reduces the coefficient of friction at high temperatures and significantly increases hardness. At the same time, too little binder reduces the pad’s durability [51,52]. Resins are the most commonly used binders in brake pad production. Numerical Simulation of the Elastic Behavior of the Automotive Brake Disc in Dry Sliding Contact With the Pads

- During braking and when the disk brought into contact with the brake pads which represent the friction body, mechanical stresses are imposed at the contact zone. All physical parameters (temperature, pressure speed and mechanical characteristics, and tribological conditions change over time), heat from friction generated at the interface, and temperature may exceed the critical value. All these problems that allowed us to do this study which concerns the numerical simulation by finite elements of a mechanical torque in dry sliding contact with motor vehicle disk/brake pads at the moment of stop braking using the ANSYS calculation code 14.5 which is based on the finite element method with its friction contact management algorithms. This behavior was analyzed in the transient case in terms of equivalent stresses and deformations (Von Mises) as a function of the braking conditions ( the type of loading, the speed of rotation of a disk, the pressure force applied to the brake pads, the coefficient of friction between the disk and the pads), and the thermal conditions (the temperature of the disk, and the heat flux in the disk, and the heat exchange by convection over the entire surface of the disk), the geometrical characteristics of the disk pads assembly and the position of the pads with respect to the brake disk and the mechanical parameters assembly and the position of the pads with respect to the brake disk and the mechanical parameters ( Young’s modulus, density, Poisson coefficient). This analysis allows us to see the behavior of the disk and the pads in contact and to recognize these damages in order to find the optimal technological solutions that will meet the needs of the engineer responsible for the design of the braking system, in particular the disk-pads torque, and to improve this system and make it more reliable and for an optimal and economical choice of the disk and pads well resist heat.

The phenomenon of friction between two surfaces that slide on each other when there is contact between two solids leads to a loss of mechanical energy that is transformed into heat. Composites which are having a good strength to less weight ratio can be applied to replace the conventionally used engineering materials. Natural fiber constitutes good properties nearly equal to that of artificial fibers. In many applications natural fiber can be applied and also it is an in expensive material. These natural fibers are extracted from agro wastes and residues obtained from agro products. It is a cost effective fiber for some specific application. A recent research on micron level investigation of particulate composites is becoming popular in both artificial and natural fiber [5, 6]. Normally artificial fibers such as carbon and glass fiber are widely used in various engineering application since it has good mechanical strength and thermal properties. These had a great disadvantage which can lead to environmental problems in disposal by incineration. In the case of natural fibre it is an environment friendly composite.

In this bagasse and palm kernel shell fibre are used for the fabrication of hybrid natural composite. The bagasse is a natural fibre which is obtained from the sugarcane extract while the palm kernel shell fibre is extracted from palm [7, 8]. Taguchi Method Optimization of Operating Parameters for Automotive Disc Brake Pad Wear

The friction pair, disc, and pad in a braking system are in a delicate balance, with the pad being a complex combination of constituents that provides predictable characteristics, including a known and consistent friction level. In this investigation, L25 orthogonal array with arranged control factors is used for the design of experiment. Taguchi design, orthogonal array, S/N ratio and variance analysis (ANOVA) are used to explore the effect of factors like applied load, sliding speed and track or interface diameter on wear rate of brake pad friction material. In dry sliding conditions, wear tests are performed on the pin‐on‐disc tribometer with different load values (25‐125

N), sliding speeds (300‐1500 rpm) and track diameter values (40‐120 mm). ANOVA results stated that applied load is the most effective with 48.27 %, track diameter is 25 % and sliding speed is 19.23 % on wear rate of pad friction material. In order to obtain the minimum friction material wear rate, the optimum operating parameters have been identified as applied load is 25 N, sliding speed 1500 rpm and track diameter 60 mm. The computed and experimental values for pad material wear rate are adhere closer to 1.93 % of deviations only.

On the Morphological and Tribological Characterization of Green Automotive Brake Pads Developed from Waste Thais Coronata Seashells

In this study, morphological and tribological analyses (optical microscopy, scanning electron microscopy as well as friction and wear tests) were used to investigate the properties of newly developed, non-toxic organic brakepads. The green automotive brake pads were developed from wastes Thais Coronata seashell reinforcement materials. The energy-dispersive X-ray spectrometer (EDX) was used to determine the chemical composition of the developed samples. Similar analyses were conducted on two commercial (control) samples for comparative purposes. EDX analysis showed the presence of toxic heavy metals (7 - 40%Sb, 6.44 -12.88%Ti) in the commercial (control) samples, unlike the green brake pad samples. The friction coefficient of the developed sample was obtained to be 0.584 while the commercial samples were 0.106 and 0.196. The tribological results show that the developed samples can maintain a superior frictional performance compared to the control samples and can be installed on heavy-duty automobiles. Optical microscopy results for samples of different particle sizes show that the wear depth increases with increase in the particle size of the reinforcement materials. Also, the presence of wear debris, friction films, and plateaus was more evident on the deformed surfaces of the commercial samples than on the deformed surfaces of the developed brake pad samples.

Room and High-Temperature Wear Behaviour of Al-Based MMCs against an Automotive Brake Pad

Aluminium metal matrix composites are promising materials for automotive brake discs, and it is critical to assess their wear performance in different braking conditions. This article presents the wear behaviour of aluminiumbased composites with different Al-Si matrix alloys added with nickel and copper to retain mechanical strength at high temperatures. The wear tests were conducted at room and high temperatures (250 and 400 °C) to simulate different braking conditions on a pin-on-plate tribometer. The coefficient of friction is in the range of 0.15–0.17 for all materials at room temperature. The specific wear rates of the brake pad and the disc materials indicate that material transfer occurs from the brake pad to the metal counterpart. Microscopy investigations of the wear tracks confirm the material transfer on the composites. It protects the composite surface from wear damage and maintains a stable coefficient of friction. To translate these results into real-world scenarios, the findings of this study suggest that aluminium-based metal matrix composite brake discs have a longer product lifespan compared to the grey cast iron brake discs; the brake pads for the composites would be the components to need replacement due to wear during the product life instead of the brake discs.

Received: 29 November 2024 Revised: 27 December 2024 Accepted: 31 December 2024 Published: 6 January 2025 Keywords: aluminium; metal matrix composite; wear; friction; tribology; microscopy 1. Introduction The development of lightweight solutions is becoming increasingly urgent every year to reduce pollution due to transport in terms of fuel consumption, CO2 emissions [1], and particulate matter (PM) emissions [2,3]. The latter is the focus of the new Euro 7 regulation, which sets for the first time a limit for PM10 (particulate matter below 10 µm in diameter) emission from brake wear [4]. Grey cast iron (GCI) brake rotors contribute to generating non-exhaust PM emissions owing to their poor wear and corrosion resistance, and mechanical braking is seldom used in the electric vehicles that now penetrate the global market. Considering these aspects, efforts have been made to substitute grey cast iron in heavy components, such as brake discs and pistons, with aluminium-based metal matrix composites (MMCs) reinforced with ceramic particles. The interest in Al-MMCs for automotive applications began at the beginning of the century [5–7], with a focus on the wear performance by Llorca [8] and Louis [9], and has increased in recent years. Dolata et al. [10] investigated the possibility of using Al-MMCs reinforced with silicon carbide (SiC) particles in piston-rings-cylinder liner assembly. The authors reported that the Al-MMCs showed significantly better tribological properties than the reference material and could be used for the studied applications. Awe and Thomas [11] presented the potential of Al-based MMC for automotive brake discs, particularly for electric vehicles, thanks to their excellent durability in terms of wear and corrosion resistance. Several factors influence tribology in MMCs: matrix alloy composition [12,13], reinforcement fraction [14] and size [15], wear conditions like load [16] and sliding speed [6], and temperature [8].
